$comment: The declared half of the dashboard's data. The other half is derived from
the repository by scripts/generate.mjs, which also VALIDATES this file:
every test named below must exist as a real Go test function, every file
must exist, and every enum value must be known. The build fails otherwise.
That is what stops this file becoming a second place to write things that
are not true. It cannot stop a wrong summary being written next to a real
test name -- nothing can -- but it does stop a guarantee citing evidence
declared - written by a human here, reference-checked by the generator
derived  - computed from the repository at build time
ci       - snapshot of a CI run, carries its own timestamp
runtime  - only knowable on a host running Nim; never available here

project.name: Nim
project.tagline: A local process between an MCP client and the MCP servers it uses.
project.currentPhase: Budgets (M5) and human approval (M6) landed: per-session caps on allowed calls, and ask rules that hold a call for nim approve with its real arguments
project.statusNote: Nim decides per (agent, connector, tool) against allow and deny rules in SQLite -- most specific wins, deny beats allow at equal specificity, no rule means allow -- records every call, every rule change and every enrolment change in one hash chain, and configures Claude Code, Cursor and Claude Desktop to go through it with nim init. Nothing has ever been executed on Windows.

ciSnapshot.$comment: Snapshot, not live. Staleness is computed against the commit being built.

runtime.$comment: Deliberately empty. See the note rendered on the Overview.
runtime.reason: Nim is local-first. The journal, enrolled agents, connectors and the daemon all live on the machine running Nim. A hosted page cannot see them, and shipping them to one would break the sync contract in docs/milestones.md. `nim console` serves that state over loopback, which is where it belongs.

nodes.label: MCP client
nodes.note: Spawns one relay per configured server. Its own executable is what an agent identity is derived from.

nodes.label: nim serve
nodes.note: Forwards every byte untouched. Asks the daemon before forwarding a tools/call and waits.

nodes.label: nim daemon
nodes.note: Decides, holds credentials, owns SQLite. Verifies its peers and is verified by them.

nodes.label: MCP server
nodes.note: Untrusted by assumption: code the operator did not write, running as the same user.

nodes.label: Remote resource
nodes.note: Outside Nim entirely. Nim never sees this hop.

layers.name: Agent identity
layers.detail: Enrolled and derived from the kernel, recorded on session.start, and every enrolment change is an agent.add or agent.remove entry in the chain. Two windows of one program are the same agent.

layers.name: Policy
layers.detail: Allow and deny rules in SQLite, per agent and per connector, with defaults; one precedence function decides and nim policy explain shows it. Changed only through the daemon and recorded in the chain.

layers.name: Credential access
layers.detail: Secrets in the OS store, released only for the connector's registered command.

layers.name: Peer verification
layers.detail: Both ends of the socket verify each other by kernel-resolved executable identity. Unsupported on Windows.

layers.name: Journal
layers.detail: Append-only and hash-chained. Integrity, not authenticity — the chain is unkeyed.

layers.name: SQLite
layers.detail: Source of truth for the journal, connectors, agents and rules. The only thing an authorization decision reads.

guarantees.title: Both ends of the daemon socket verify each other
guarantees.statement: A process that is not this binary cannot speak on the daemon socket, in either direction. The daemon checks its callers; the relay and every management command check whatever is listening before sending a byte.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It answers "is this Nim", not "is this a relay the operator meant to run". Anything able to execute the binary passes it.

guarantees.title: Peer identity is the running image, not a filename
guarantees.statement: Identity comes from the kernel's view of what a process is executing: /proc/<pid>/exe on linux, the vnode behind the process's own mapping on darwin. Replacing the file at a peer's launch path does not defeat it.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It is not code-signing identity. A rebuild is a different inode and therefore a different program. Not implemented on Windows at all.

guarantees.title: A credential is only injected into the command it was registered for
guarantees.statement: A connector names the one server its secret may reach. The daemon returns that command; the relay spawns it. A caller naming another connector gets that connector's real server, which is not a way to read anything.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The registered argv is spawned through normal PATH resolution, so a caller that already controls PATH can front-run the binary name.

guarantees.title: A secret never becomes a command-line argument
guarantees.statement: Secrets are read from stdin or a no-echo prompt, stored in the OS credential store, and reach a connector only through its environment.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The connector receives the secret in its environment and can do what it likes with it. On Linux any same-user process can read /proc/<pid>/environ.

guarantees.title: Every way of not getting a decision is a denial
guarantees.statement: No daemon, a slow daemon, a closed socket, a reply that does not match the question, or a journal write that failed — each denies. There is no path on which a tools/call reaches a connector without a decision behind it.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It protects calls that go through Nim. Nothing stops a client being reconfigured to spawn the MCP server directly.

guarantees.title: The journal is append-only in fact, not by convention
guarantees.statement: A call produces two immutable entries rather than one row that is updated. Nothing in the write path updates an entry. Configuration that decides what may happen -- rules and enrolments -- is changed in one transaction with the entry that records the change.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Append-only as far as this code is concerned. Nothing stops another process opening the file and writing to it.

guarantees.title: Altering an entry breaks the chain
guarantees.statement: Each entry's hash covers its contents and its position, so an edit made by anything that does not recompute the chain is detected by nim verify.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: INTEGRITY, NOT AUTHENTICITY. The chain is unkeyed. Anyone who can write to nim.db can recompute every hash from the genesis and the result verifies cleanly.

guarantees.title: A recorded head detects truncate-and-recompute
guarantees.statement: nim verify --expect-head looks for the recorded head IN the chain. Finding it establishes that nothing at or before it was rewritten; not finding it anywhere is what distinguishes a rewrite from ordinary growth.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Only covers what was committed before the head you recorded, and only if you recorded one somewhere Nim cannot reach.

guarantees.title: A journal spanning schema versions still verifies
guarantees.statement: Verification dispatches on the version each entry stored: v1 before agent existed, v2 with it, v3 with the enrolment fields, v4 with a budget's cap. A mixed chain checks out end to end, and a table an earlier build created is rebuilt to the current definition on open with every row copied verbatim, so the chain that comes out is the chain that went in.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: An entry claiming a version this build does not know is refused rather than checked. That is intended, but it means a downgrade cannot read a newer journal.

guarantees.title: An agent identity cannot be claimed by the agent
guarantees.statement: The daemon derives the agent from the kernel: socket peer, its parent, the file that parent executes. There is no agent field on the wire, and one executable is enrolled under one name only, so the derivation has exactly one answer.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Two windows of one program are the same agent. Enrolment is as privileged as running Nim; since 2026-09-15 every enrolment change is an entry in the chain, so it is visible afterwards, not prevented.

guarantees.title: A connection may only speak for sessions it opened
guarantees.statement: Peer identity cannot tell one run of Nim from another; session ownership stops one connection appending entries under a session another opened. A session id names one session: a start under an id that is live on any connection, or that the journal already holds, is refused and the connection closed.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Anything running this binary can still open its own session and report whatever it likes about it.

guarantees.title: A client cannot tell it is going through Nim
guarantees.statement: Everything that is not a tools/call is forwarded as the exact bytes that arrived, and a real MCP client run direct and through Nim observes the same tool list, schemas, unicode, a 512 KiB payload, error propagation and ping. Unit tests cover the framing; tools/relay-rig proves it with a real client, re-run on 2026-09-15 against the current binary, including the two cases that must differ through Nim.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The rig has run under both the initialize and the server/discover handshake. The rig has run locally and on darwin only; the relay-rig CI job exists but has not yet run on GitHub's runners, so linux stays partial and windows unverified.

guarantees.title: Policy lives in SQLite and every change is in the chain
guarantees.statement: A rule is added or removed through the daemon, over the peer-verified socket, in one transaction with the rule.add or rule.remove entry recording it. The chain never says a rule exists that does not, and no rule exists the chain does not know about. config.toml carries no policy, and a file that still does is refused rather than read past.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Anything able to run the binary as this user can add or remove a rule, exactly as it can enrol an agent; the entry is what makes that visible, not what prevents it.

guarantees.title: Two agents against one connector receive different verdicts
guarantees.statement: A decision is (agent, connector, tool). A rule scoped to an enrolled agent applies to sessions the daemon derived as that agent and to no other; a rule scoped to a connector applies to sessions started for it. The record distinguishes the agents on their session.start entries. Proven with two real client programs spawning real relays, not only in-process.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: A session no enrolment matched meets only the rules that name no agent (D-002). With deny rules alone that is the ceiling every session had before agents existed; with a default deny and an agent-scoped allow it is a denial -- enrolment is then what grants, and docs/decisions/0003 says so.

guarantees.title: A tools/call travels only if Nim read it unambiguously
guarantees.statement: Objects are read by the exact bytes of each key, an object naming a key twice is refused, and a tools/call whose params or name cannot be read as one string is refused before the daemon is asked. What the daemon decides on and the journal records is the name the server will act on.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Keys inside params.arguments are the tool's business and are digested, never interpreted. A frame refused for a repeated key is not answered, because which id to answer under is the same question. Parser disagreements other than duplicate keys and case-variant keys -- NaN, Infinity -- were already refused as malformed.

guarantees.title: Enrolment changes are entries in the chain
guarantees.statement: nim agent add and nim agent remove write the enrolment and an agent.add or agent.remove entry in one SQLite transaction. The entry carries the name, the enrolled path and the resolved identity (schema_version 3), so re-enrolling a name against another executable -- which moves every rule scoped to that name -- is visible in the record beside the rules it moved.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Visible, not prevented: anything that can run the binary as this user can still re-enrol a name. The identity recorded is device and inode, which a reboot or a reinstall can change; nim agent list reports the enrolment STALE when it no longer matches.

guarantees.title: One function decides, and explain shows its work
guarantees.statement: Among the rules matching a call, the most specific wins (an exact tool over a default, a named agent or connector over an unnamed one); at equal specificity deny beats ask beats allow (ask holds the call for a human, M6); with no matching rule the call is allowed, which is the M4 baseline. journal.Decide is that function, table-tested with no database, reused verbatim by nim policy explain, so the CLI cannot say something a real call would not do.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: No conditions on arguments and no time bounds: a rule is keyed on (agent, connector, tool) and nothing else. A budget (M5) caps how many calls a session may make once the rules allow them; it is a separate cap, not a rule. A client that genuinely names a tool `*` matches a default rule like any other exact name would.

guarantees.title: nim init rewrites only the servers it wraps
guarantees.statement: Unrelated top-level keys, an entry's other fields, env values and the file's own key order survive nim init untouched; only a wrapped or repointed entry's command and args change. Nothing is written without --write, --write copies the file to a 0600 backup first and writes atomically, and --undo restores the backup the same way. A config that is a symlink is written through, so a dotfiles-managed file stays managed, and no two backups ever share a name.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Untouched values are re-indented to match the rest of the file, so byte-for-byte whitespace is not preserved -- only content, position and key order are. Only stdio servers are wrapped; entries with a url are left alone and said so.

guarantees.title: nim doctor never starts the daemon it reports on
guarantees.statement: nim doctor dials the daemon socket without the auto-start every other command uses, so an unreachable daemon is reported as a warning rather than being brought up as a side effect of asking, and nothing doctor does writes anywhere.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The warning does not distinguish a daemon that has never run from one that crashed a moment ago; both read the same way. Which checks are FAIL and which are WARN is a judgement, stated in doctor.go.

guarantees.title: nim version reports what build it is
guarantees.statement: nim version prints version, commit, build time, platform and Go version in one documented shape, stamped by the release workflow's -ldflags at build time.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: A binary built any other way (go build, go run) reports unknown for commit and build time; the shape holds, the values are only meaningful for a release archive. No release has been published yet.

guarantees.title: A budget caps the allowed calls one session may make
guarantees.statement: Once the rules allow a call, every budget whose scope matches is weighed against that session's call.request entries with decision allow or approved; a call that would exceed a matching budget's cap is denied, with a reason naming the budget, and the decision is written before the relay is told. A budget that exists is shown wherever the policy is shown: nim policy list, nim status and the console.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: A budget never grants: it cannot turn a rule's deny into anything else. It counts decisions, not outcomes, so a call the relay gave up waiting on still counts. It does not survive a restarted relay: a new session starts with a fresh count.

guarantees.title: A held call is shown to the human as its real parameters, and decided before the relay acts
guarantees.statement: A call an ask rule wins is held in the daemon's memory and answered pending; nim approve prints the exact params.arguments bytes the relay read, pretty-printed with every byte shown as itself, never a summary and never text a model wrote about the call. The decision -- approved or rejected -- is written to the journal before the relay is told, and on approval the relay forwards the original frame byte for byte. An approve is refused until that report has arrived, so nothing can be approved before the bytes exist on the daemon's side.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Who approves is anyone who can run nim as this user; the socket cannot tell an operator from a model that has been given a shell. The arguments are the model's to write: what is shown is what was sent, which may itself be misleading. A held call does not survive a daemon killed outright.

attacks.name: Name a connector, supply your own command, read the credential
attacks.evidence: Reproduced live against a real build; the token printed. Fixed by the connector command binding.

attacks.name: Ask for a credential from a process that is not Nim
attacks.evidence: A raw socket client that speaks the protocol correctly is still refused: the daemon verifies the peer's running image at accept, before it reads a single request byte. Denial does not depend on the request being malformed.

attacks.name: Write forged entries to the journal from a non-Nim process
attacks.evidence: A python socket client wrote a fabricated session and an allowed delete_repository call. Fixed by authorizing the event path.

attacks.name: Obtain a decision from a non-Nim process
attacks.evidence: Connection closed before any decision is produced.

attacks.name: Report calls under a session another connection opened
attacks.evidence: Refused, and the connection is closed rather than merely erroring. Found by the 2026-09-14 audit: the check exempted session.start itself, so a second connection could re-announce a live session's id and then report calls, outcomes and an end into it; reproduced against the daemon in a scratch copy. A session id now names one session, daemon-wide and for all time -- live on any connection, or ever recorded, and a second start is refused.

attacks.name: Bind the socket first and impersonate the daemon
attacks.evidence: As the daemon, a python script had the relay spawn a command of its choosing, allowed a denied call, and harvested tool names. Introduced by the merge; fixed by verifying both ends. The 2026-09-14 audit found the management commands still trusted the socket: nim connector set would have written the plaintext secret to an impostor. Every command now dials through one verified path. nim status used to report such a listener as running; it now performs the same verification and says NOT NIM (2026-09-15).

attacks.name: As an impostor, harvest tool names and argument digests
attacks.evidence: Verification happens before a byte is written, so the impostor learns nothing.

attacks.name: Defeat peer identity by swapping the file at the peer's launch path
attacks.evidence: A genuine nc process passed peer identity with no race. Fixed by resolving the running image instead of a path. Mutation-verified.

attacks.name: Exhaust daemon memory with an unterminated line
attacks.evidence: 200 MiB in 0.2s from one unauthenticated connection. Capped at 1 MiB.

attacks.name: Bypass the rules
attacks.evidence: A call a rule names never reaches the connector; the rules are read from SQLite at decision time and exact names only. The list used to live in config.toml, which is F-004.

attacks.name: Smuggle a tools/call inside a JSON-RPC batch
attacks.evidence: Batch carrying a tools/call is refused whole.

attacks.name: Smuggle a call in a frame Go cannot parse but the server can
attacks.evidence: A frame Go cannot parse is not forwarded, and neither is a frame carrying more than one message. The rule is that anything the relay cannot fully understand does not reach the connector -- a parser disagreement must not become a way to move a tools/call past the decision point. That rule had a hole until 2026-09-14: see the duplicate-key row.

attacks.name: Kill the daemon to disable enforcement
attacks.evidence: Every tools/call is denied while the daemon is gone. Killing the enforcement point removes the ability to call tools, not the enforcement -- which is the whole content of the fail-closed decision recorded in docs/decisions/0001.

attacks.name: Truncate the journal's tail
attacks.evidence: Detected ONLY with --expect-head against a head recorded elsewhere. Undetectable otherwise, because the chain is unkeyed.

attacks.name: Rewrite the whole journal from the genesis
attacks.evidence: Not defended. Nothing in the chain is secret, so anyone who can write nim.db can recompute every hash and the result verifies cleanly. Only an externally recorded head covers any of it.

attacks.name: Pass --expect-head a head the journal has grown past
attacks.evidence: Previously reported ordinary growth as 'entries have been removed'. A check that cries wolf stops being read.

attacks.name: Claim an agent identity on the wire
attacks.evidence: There is no agent field on Event; the serialised message is asserted not to contain one.

attacks.name: Use a stale enrolment after the executable is replaced
attacks.evidence: A replaced file no longer matches; the enrolment is reported STALE rather than silently adopting the new file.

attacks.name: Land a new file on a deleted enrolment's inode number
attacks.evidence: Inode reuse is real: ext4 hands back the number it just freed, observed in CI. A running process holds its inode so the runtime path is safe; a PERSISTED enrolment whose file was deleted could be matched by an unrelated later file. No test covers the adversarial case.

attacks.name: Overwrite another agent's enrolment
attacks.evidence: Anything that can run the nim binary as this user can re-enrol any name against any executable, and now that rules are scoped to enrolments that moves the name's rules to the new program. Since 2026-09-15 the re-enrolment is an agent.add entry in the chain carrying the new identity, beside the rules it moved: not prevented -- the same-user threat model grants it -- but recorded where nim verify covers it.

attacks.name: Overwrite a connector's registered command
attacks.evidence: Possible, but destructive rather than exfiltrating: connector.set requires a secret, so an attacker replaces the credential with their own rather than reading the existing one.

attacks.name: Front-run the registered command through PATH
attacks.evidence: The registered argv is spawned through normal PATH resolution. A caller that already controls PATH can place its own binary first. Closing it needs the daemon to spawn the connector itself.

attacks.name: Leave a connector running after the relay dies
attacks.evidence: The downstream is the relay's child. When the relay exits or is asked to stop (SIGTERM, SIGINT) it stops the connector: closes its stdin, waits, asks it to terminate, then kills it. Found by the 2026-09-14 audit: the signal path used to exit without touching the child, so a connector that ignored stdin outlived the relay with whatever credential it held. Still open: a relay killed outright (SIGKILL) runs nothing, and then only a connector that reads its stdin notices.

attacks.name: Restart the daemon mid-session
attacks.evidence: Sessions left open are closed by the daemon when a connection drops, and calls fail closed. Not exercised as a deliberate restart-under-load test.

attacks.name: Run a new client against an old daemon
attacks.evidence: Replacing the binary in place while a daemon runs breaks every operation until it is restarted, with an opaque 'reading response: EOF'. Fails closed, but the message tells the operator nothing.

attacks.name: Open the journal from two processes at once
attacks.evidence: Found by CI: syncViews dropped and recreated a view unsynchronised. Now one immediate transaction; regression test fails 5/5 against the old code.

attacks.name: Provoke races under contention
attacks.evidence: Three real races found and fixed with reproductions: split-brain daemon start, torn credential read, BUSY_SNAPSHOT. Suite runs -race -shuffle.

attacks.name: Feed the daemon malformed JSON
attacks.evidence: Malformed messages are recorded as an anomaly and skipped; oversized ones are refused before the full parse.

attacks.name: Reuse a JSON-RPC id for two in-flight calls
attacks.evidence: Recorded as a duplicate_id anomaly. The second answer still cannot be matched to the right request, and nothing prevents the situation.

attacks.name: Crash between decision and forward
attacks.evidence: No test. The known window is documented: the relay gives up after 2s and SQLite's busy timeout is 5s, so a contended write can land after a denial, leaving an allow for a call that never happened. It reads as pending, never as executed.

attacks.name: Crash while relaying a response
attacks.evidence: No test covers this. A crash midway through relaying a response would leave the client with a truncated frame and the journal with a call.request but no call.response. Reasoning says that reads as an unfinished call rather than a successful one, which is the safe direction, but reasoning is not a test and this row does not claim otherwise.

attacks.name: Power loss mid-commit
attacks.evidence: synchronous=FULL is asserted but never tested against real hardware loss.

attacks.name: Cross a privilege boundary
attacks.evidence: There is no privilege boundary to cross. Everything runs as one OS user by design; that is the premise, not a gap.

attacks.name: Act as an agent nobody enrolled
attacks.evidence: Bound by the rules that name no agent, and nothing else: D-002, resolved in docs/decisions/0002 for deny rules and again in docs/decisions/0003 for the allow model. With deny rules alone an unenrolled program has the ceiling every session had before agents existed; with nim policy default deny plus an agent-scoped allow it is denied by the default -- enrolment is then what grants.

attacks.name: Name a connector that does not exist
attacks.evidence: No connector configured is the ordinary case: spawn with no credential.

attacks.name: Call a tool no policy mentions
attacks.evidence: Allowed, unless a default deny is set. Since M4.5 rules can grant as well as refuse: nim policy default deny closes everything and nim policy allow reopens one tool for one agent or connector. With no default rule, anything no rule names still passes, which is the M4 baseline a fresh install keeps. Partial because the closed posture is something the operator opts into, not the default.

attacks.name: A same-user process that already ran code
attacks.evidence: This is the threat model's adversary and it is only partly contained. It can run the nim binary, enrol agents, overwrite connectors, and open its own sessions. What it cannot do is read another connector's credential or forge entries without running Nim.

attacks.name: Manipulate symlinks and paths
attacks.evidence: The path-swap test builds the attack out of symlinks: it launches a peer through a symlink it controls, then re-points that symlink at Nim's own binary so the launch path names Nim while the running process is genuinely something else. Identity comes from the kernel's view of the running image, so the swap changes nothing.

attacks.name: Read a credential from the connector's environment
attacks.evidence: By design the connector receives the secret in its environment, and it inherits the relay's whole environment. On Linux any same-user process can read /proc/<pid>/environ. Closing it needs Nim to hold the credential and proxy the request.

attacks.name: Make this dashboard state something untrue
attacks.evidence: Red-teamed deliberately on 2026-08-12 with sixteen attempts: forged statuses, relabelled milestones, closed decisions, duplicated ids, invented runtime data, secrets and local paths in prose, overridden test counts. Fourteen got through and are now refused, each with a regression test; the two that appeared to work never had — derived facts are computed after the declared ones are spread in, so a hand-written count cannot win. The build also scans every byte of the published output, not just the data file. What remains undetectable is a wrong summary written next to a real test name, and a platform column resting on a test that compiles there without proving anything.

attacks.name: Reach something other than the dashboard on the public deployment
attacks.evidence: Audited from outside on 2026-08-12 against all three intended hostnames. Refused: .env and .env.local, .git, .vercel/project.json, builds.json and config.json, package.json, vercel.json, next.config.mjs, data/state.json, generate.mjs, nim.db, .nim/, engine sources, .DS_Store, node_modules -- all 404. No source maps exist and no chunk references one. Path traversal returns 400 or a generic edge error. POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH/TRACE all 405. /_src redirects to Vercel's source viewer, which demands a login. No secret shape, token, JWT or local path appears in any served byte, and no journal data: no chain hash, prev_hash, chain_seq, machine_id or session id. Partial rather than pass because sixteen historical deployment URLs and one stale branch alias also answer publicly -- see F-012 -- serving Vercel failure pages and an abandoned placeholder rather than this dashboard.

attacks.name: Smuggle a tools/call behind a repeated or case-variant key
attacks.evidence: Reproduced against the real relay on 2026-09-14, before the fix: `"method":5,"method":"tools/call"` and `"method":"tools/call","Method":"ping"` both reached the connector with no decision, no journal entry and no anomaly, because Go's typed decoder matches keys case-insensitively, lets the last match win, and carries on past a member of the wrong type -- while every mainstream server reads tools/call. Objects are now read by exact key; a repeated key is refused as an anomaly, and a case-variant key is simply a different key, to Nim as to the server.

attacks.name: Name one tool to the daemon and another to the server
attacks.evidence: Same root cause, worse consequence: `"name":"delete_repository","Name":"list_repos"` had the daemon decide on list_repos, the journal record it, and the server run delete_repository. A tools/call is now decided on the exact-key name or refused before the daemon is asked; a call with no readable name is refused too, where it used to be decided as tool "" and allowed.

attacks.name: Change the rules by editing config.toml
attacks.evidence: Nothing an authorization decision reads is in config.toml any more. A file that still carries a [policy] section is refused by every command, with the way forward in the message, rather than read past -- a deny list an operator believes is enforced and is not would be the worst way for the move to go unnoticed. Unknown keys are refused for the same reason: [polciy] used to deny nothing, silently.

attacks.name: Change the rules without leaving a journal entry
attacks.evidence: A rule and its rule.add or rule.remove entry are one SQLite transaction: a trigger that refuses the entry leaves no rule, and one that refuses the rule leaves no entry. The entry is hashed into the chain like a call, so editing it afterwards breaks verification. Since 2026-09-15 the same holds for enrolments (agent.add, agent.remove).

attacks.name: Bind the socket first and receive the secret from nim connector set
attacks.evidence: Found by reading, not by running: the relay verified the daemon before sending a byte, but nim connector set, nim agent add and their siblings dialled the socket path and trusted whatever answered -- and connector set carries the plaintext secret. Every management command now goes through the one dial that verifies the peer, and the CLI refuses to talk to a process that is not Nim.

attacks.name: Read the console from another site through DNS rebinding
attacks.evidence: nim console binds loopback, but a bind address is not a name: a page on any site can have its own hostname resolve to 127.0.0.1 and then read /api/snapshot, /api/events and every session as if they were its own origin. The console now answers only to a loopback Host -- localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 -- and refuses any other name with 421 before a route runs.

attacks.name: Read a connector's secret through the console
attacks.evidence: The console's /api/policy lists rules, enrolments and connectors from the read-only journal handle. There is no secret to leak: the credential lives in the OS store and the journal holds only the env key name and the authorized command. A test asserts the endpoint's JSON never carries a key named secret or a credential value, and the route keeps the console's GET-only and loopback-Host rules.

attacks.name: Make nim init damage a client's configuration
attacks.evidence: nim init writes nothing without --write; with it, the original is copied to a 0600 backup first and the new file is written to a temporary name and renamed, so a crash leaves either the old file or the new one. A file that does not parse, or is not a JSON object, is refused. Unrelated keys, env values and key order are preserved; an entry already through Nim is left alone rather than wrapped twice; --undo restores the backup atomically.

attacks.name: Enrol a second name against the operator's client binary
attacks.evidence: Found by the 2026-09-15 review, reproduced in a scratch test: nothing stopped two names from enrolling one executable, and the lookup that derives a session's agent had no order, so after the operator re-enrolled their own client the other name's rules -- allow rules included -- could apply to it. One executable is now one agent: a second name is refused naming the first, the lookup is ordered, and ownership moves only when the holder removes its enrolment, which the chain records.

attacks.name: Read a secret from nim init's own output
attacks.evidence: Found by the 2026-09-15 review, reproduced with the built binary: the before/after a dry run printed included the entry's env block, where client configs keep their API tokens, so a plain nim init put real secrets into terminal scrollback. The preview now shows env keys with every value hidden; the file that is written keeps them untouched.

attacks.name: Speak the newer server/discover handshake so the client cannot parse Nim's refusals
attacks.evidence: Reproduced on 2026-09-15 with fastmcp 4.0.3 against the unmodified relay: a connector that answers server/discover moves the client onto the 2026-07-28 revision, where every result must name its resultType, and Nim's hand-written refusal did not -- the client raised a local ValidationError instead of reading 'Nim denied this call', which is not a refusal from where the model sits. Nim now watches server/discover as it watches initialize and writes each refusal in the dialect the session negotiated. Re-run after the fix: ToolError with Nim's text under both handshakes; the rig's denial case runs under both.

attacks.name: Exhaust a budget, then keep calling
attacks.evidence: Through a real relay against a real daemon, a budget of 2 allowed exactly two calls and refused the third; the refusal was journaled with the budget named in the reason. A session's own refusals do not spend the budget, and a budget cannot make a call a rule denies pass. Restarting the relay starts a new session with a fresh count, which is the documented scope of a budget, not a bypass of it.

attacks.name: Approve your own call from the model
attacks.evidence: Blocked only by circumstance, and stated as such rather than claimed further: the daemon's approval purpose is reachable only through the nim binary, which peer identity verifies at accept, so a model with no way to execute commands cannot reach nim approve at all; the relay's own connection is bound to the events purpose and refused an approval.decide. A model that has been given a shell runs nim approve exactly as the operator would, and nothing on the socket tells the two apart. docs/decisions/0005-human-approval.md and the threat model say so.

attacks.name: Leak a held call's real arguments into the journal, a log line, or the operator's terminal
attacks.evidence: A held call's arguments live only in the daemon's pending registry. Checked directly: with a distinctive marker in the arguments, the database and the daemon's captured log output never contain it, and the Response type's String never prints it. nim approve shows every byte as itself: an escape sequence or a bidirectional override in an argument is printed as its escape, so a terminal cannot be made to hide or reorder what the human is approving.

attacks.name: Get a call approved before the daemon has received its arguments
attacks.evidence: Found by the 2026-09-15 review of the merged M6 code and reproduced in a scratch test: with the relay's call.arguments report withheld, approval.decide accepted an approve, journaled it and told the relay, and nim approve showed the call as one with no arguments. The daemon now records whether the report has arrived and refuses an approve until it has; a reject goes through regardless; a second report never replaces the first.

findings.title: Two enrolments could share one executable, and the lookup between them had no order
findings.problem: nim_agents was unique on name only, and the query that derives a session's agent from the relay's parent image had no ORDER BY. A same-user process could enrol a second name against the operator's client binary; a routine re-enrolment by the operator then changed which row the lookup returned.
findings.impact: Every rule scoped to the operator's agent, allow rules included, could silently apply to the wrong name, with a chain that verified perfectly. Found by review on 2026-09-15 before anything shipped.
findings.evidence: Reproduced in a scratch test by the reviewer: after remove-and-re-add of the operator's name, the lookup answered with the intruder's. Fixed: AddAgent refuses a second name for an enrolled image inside its transaction, the lookup is ordered, and the daemon's refusal names the enrolment in the way.
findings.nextAction: None. Ownership of an image moves only when its holder removes the enrolment, and that is an agent.remove entry.

findings.title: nim init printed env values in its dry-run diff
findings.problem: The before/after preview rendered the whole entry, env block included, though env never changes. Client configs keep API tokens there.
findings.impact: A plain nim init, the command an operator runs first and pipes or shares, wrote real secrets to stdout.
findings.evidence: Reproduced by the reviewer with fake tokens in a fixture config. Fixed: the preview shows env keys with values hidden.
findings.nextAction: None. The preview hides every env value and a test holds it to that; the file written keeps the values untouched, which a second test holds it to.

findings.title: Two nim init --write runs in one second shared a backup name
findings.problem: Backup names carried a second-resolution timestamp and were written with os.WriteFile, so the second run overwrote the first run's backup of the true original.
findings.impact: nim init --undo could no longer reach the original file after a quick retry or a setup script wrapping two clients back to back.
findings.evidence: Reproduced by the reviewer with the built binary. Fixed: nanosecond names, created exclusively, with a numbered suffix if a name is somehow taken; the path returned is the one written.
findings.nextAction: None. Backup names now carry nanoseconds and are created exclusively; a taken name gets a numbered suffix and the path reported is the one written.

findings.title: The relay could wait on its connector from two goroutines at once
findings.problem: stopDownstream was reachable from the signal handler and from the normal exit path with no guard, and two concurrent Waits on one exec.Cmd are a data race.
findings.impact: A Ctrl-C that closes the pipes and delivers the signal together could hit it; the race detector reported it under a scratch test. The connector was still terminated correctly in every run.
findings.evidence: Found by the reviewer with go test -race. Fixed: the stop runs once, guarded like finish already was, and hands both callers the same result.
findings.nextAction: None. The stop runs under a sync.Once like finish already did; the regression test drives it from two goroutines under the race detector.

findings.title: Nim's own refusals predate the result shape a newer client negotiates
findings.problem: fastmcp 4's default client mode negotiates a server/discover handshake under which every result carries a resultType field. Nim relays that traffic byte for byte, but the responses Nim writes itself -- the tool error that refuses a call (engine/internal/mcp/deny.go) -- do not carry the field, so a client in that mode fails to parse Nim's refusal instead of reading it as a tool error.
findings.impact: A refused call reaches such a client as a local validation error rather than the clear 'Nim denied this call' text, which defeats the point of answering in the shape MCP uses for tool failures. Clients on the standard MCP handshake, including the Go end-to-end tests and the rig pinned to legacy mode, are unaffected.
findings.evidence: Found on 2026-09-15 while bringing the relay rig back: fastmcp 4.0.3 in its default mode raised a ValidationError on Nim's denial; pinned to mode=legacy the rig passed. Fixed the same day: the relay watches server/discover as it watches initialize, learns the negotiated version from the proposal and the server's supportedVersions, and writes a refusal with resultType "complete" when that version is 2026-07-28 or later. Reproduced before and after with the real client: the same call now raises ToolError with Nim's text in both modes, and the rig's denial case runs under both handshakes (RESULT: IDENTICAL, darwin, 2026-09-15).
findings.nextAction: None. Older clients are sent the older shape unchanged; a future revision that changes the result shape again will need the same treatment, and the rig's default-mode case is where it would show.

findings.title: A repeated or case-variant JSON key smuggled a tools/call past the decision
findings.problem: Go's typed JSON decoder matches keys case-insensitively, lets the last of several matches win, and continues past a member of the wrong type. A frame with `"method":5,"method":"tools/call"` decoded to an empty envelope and was relayed; one with `"Method":"ping"` beside `"method":"tools/call"` read as ping; `"Name"` beside `"name"` renamed the tool the daemon decided on.
findings.impact: A tools/call reached the connector with no decision, no journal entry and no anomaly -- the one-direction guarantee did not hold -- and in the rename case the journal recorded a harmless tool while the server ran a denied one.
findings.evidence: Reproduced on 2026-09-14 against the unmodified relay: both frames reached the connector, the daemon was asked about 0 calls. Fixed by reading objects by exact key (engine/internal/mcp/mcp.go objectFields) and refusing repeated keys and unreadable calls; seven regression tests.
findings.nextAction: None. docs/journal-format.md now states the duplicate-key rule the relay applies, and that keys inside params.arguments are not interpreted.

findings.title: A second connection could start a session under another connection's id
findings.problem: The session-ownership check exempted session.start, and the set of open sessions was per connection, so a second connection could announce a start under a live id and then report calls, outcomes and an end into the first connection's session.
findings.impact: On a platform without peer verification, or after any regression of it, one relay could write into another's story. Security.md claimed session ownership held independently of peer identity; it did not.
findings.evidence: Found and reproduced in a scratch copy by the 2026-09-14 audit. Fixed: a daemon-wide registry refuses a start for an id that is live on any connection or that the journal has ever recorded, and closes the connection.
findings.nextAction: None beyond the registry. Kept on the page because 'session ownership holds on its own' was a claim the page made and the code did not back until this.

findings.title: nim connector set trusted whatever was bound to the socket
findings.problem: The relay verified the daemon's executable identity before sending it a byte; the management commands dialled the socket path and did not. nim connector set carries the plaintext secret.
findings.impact: A process that bound the socket path first -- the impostor the relay already refused -- would have been handed every secret the operator registered from then on.
findings.evidence: Found by reading engine/cmd/nim/connector.go on 2026-09-14; not reproduced live. Fixed: one verified dial (shim.DialDaemon) serves every command, and a test drives it against an impostor.
findings.nextAction: None. Kept because it is the shape of mistake to look for next time a second caller of the socket appears: every path that talks to the daemon must dial through the one that verifies it.

findings.title: The console answered to any Host header
findings.problem: nim console bound loopback but checked only the request method, so a page on another site could rebind its own name to 127.0.0.1 and read the record from the operator's browser as its own origin.
findings.impact: Tool names, connectors, session ids, digests and the chain head readable by a web page the operator happened to visit while the console ran.
findings.evidence: Found by the 2026-09-14 audit and confirmed by two independent verifiers. Fixed: requests whose Host is not a loopback name are refused with 421.
findings.nextAction: None. The Host check is the standing guard; a future console that binds anything other than loopback has to revisit it.

findings.title: Every open dropped and recreated the journal's views under a write lock
findings.problem: syncViews compared the stored view definition with the statement as written, but SQLite stores CREATE statements with the first keywords upper-cased. The comparison never matched, so the 'only when drifted' path was the only path.
findings.impact: Two opens of one file always raced on the views, which is how the concurrent-open collision (TestConcurrentOpensDoNotCollideOnViews) was reachable in the first place, and a read-only command took a write lock on every start.
findings.evidence: Reproduced on 2026-09-14: both views reported drifted immediately after creation. Fixed by comparing against the stored form; a test holds the steady state to a read.
findings.nextAction: None. The stored-form comparison is tested; a change to a view's DDL is now a one-time recreate rather than a recreate on every open.

findings.title: Enrolment changes leave no journal entry
findings.problem: A rule is journaled when it is added or removed; the enrolment it is scoped to is not. nim agent add can move a name -- and every rule scoped to it -- to a different executable with nothing in the chain saying so.
findings.impact: An audit of the rules is possible; an audit of who the rules applied to, over time, is not. Same-user threat model, so not a bypass, but the one policy input that changes silently.
findings.evidence: Fixed 2026-09-15: agent.add and agent.remove are chain entries at schema_version 3, carrying the enrolled path and the resolved identity, written in one transaction with the enrolment (AddAgent, RemoveAgent). A journal from the M4 build is rebuilt on open with its rows unchanged.
findings.nextAction: None. The enrolment a rule is scoped to now has the same history the rule has; F-006 remains what it is, a property of one OS user.

findings.title: nim log --json stopped after one page and looped on -n 0
findings.problem: The stream compared each page against the raw -n value while the journal caps a read at 1000, so -n above the cap ended after one page with exit status 0, and -n 0 never ended.
findings.impact: An export of a 3000-entry journal came back with 1000 entries and no message.
findings.evidence: Found by the 2026-09-14 audit and confirmed. Fixed: the page size is clamped to what the journal returns and -n must be positive.
findings.nextAction: None. The page size is clamped where the read is, and -n must be positive; an export now ends when the journal does.

findings.title: A connector could outlive a relay that was asked to stop
findings.problem: On SIGTERM or SIGINT the relay flushed the journal and exited without touching its child. A connector that does not read stdin -- mid-call, or on its own event loop -- kept running with whatever credential it had been given, after the journal had recorded the session as over.
findings.impact: The orphan-connector row claimed 'dies with it' on the strength of tests that never exercised the signal path.
findings.evidence: Found by the concurrency finder on 2026-09-14. Fixed: the relay stops its child on every exit path -- stdin closed, then SIGTERM, then kill -- and a test sends SIGTERM to a relay whose connector ignores stdin. SIGKILL to the relay remains what it was, and the row says so.
findings.nextAction: None for SIGTERM and SIGINT. SIGKILL to the relay remains what it was and the orphan-connector row says so; closing it needs the daemon to own the connector, which is process inversion.

findings.title: Old deployments became public along with the intended one
findings.problem: Turning deployment protection off applies to every deployment the project has ever made, not only the current one. Sixteen historical deployment URLs answer anonymously, plus a stale branch alias nim-git-m1-bootstrap-seergiiim.vercel.app left over from when the repository was connected to Vercel.
findings.impact: Fourteen serve Vercel's generic 'Deployment has failed' page, which carries a deployment id and nothing else. One serves the abandoned v0 placeholder that predates this dashboard. No secret, source, build log or local path was found in any of them -- so this is untidy rather than dangerous, and it means the promise 'only the dashboard is public' is not literally true.
findings.evidence: Enumerated all 16 deployment URLs and fetched each anonymously. 14 returned the 20331-byte failure page, 1 returned the 12888-byte v0 stub titled 'v0 App', 1 is the current dashboard. Greps for local paths, build errors, npm output and tokens across those bodies returned nothing.
findings.nextAction: Delete the historical deployments and the stale branch alias in the Vercel dashboard, so that the only thing this project serves is the page intended to be served. Needs a human: deleting deployments is destructive and is not this repository's call.

findings.title: A protected Vercel project served this page publicly anyway
findings.problem: Vercel Authentication was enabled on the project, but scoped all_except_custom_domains. Vercel treats the project's own assigned production domain (nim-blush.vercel.app) as a custom domain, so that hostname was exempt while every other URL for the same deployment was protected.
findings.impact: The full page -- every known weakness, undefended attack path and architectural limitation -- was readable by anyone at that URL, with no login, for roughly two minutes on 2026-08-12. Two of the three hostnames behaved correctly, which is what made it easy to believe the whole thing was protected.
findings.evidence: Reading the protection settings was not enough and produced a confident wrong conclusion. Fetching every hostname anonymously was: nim-seergiiim.vercel.app and the deployment URL returned 302 to vercel.com/sso-api with a 15-byte body, while nim-blush.vercel.app returned HTTP 200 with 211 KB containing 'Break Nim' and 'journal chain is unkeyed'. The deployment was removed immediately; all hostnames now return 404 with no content.
findings.nextAction: Do not deploy again until deployment protection covers all deployments rather than all_except_custom_domains. More generally: verify access control by fetching every hostname anonymously, never by reading the configuration that is supposed to provide it.

findings.title: In-place upgrade breaks a running daemon, opaquely
findings.problem: Replacing the binary while a daemon runs makes the old daemon and the new client different images, so every operation is refused.
findings.impact: All Nim operations fail until the daemon is restarted. The client sees 'nim: reading response: EOF' with no hint.
findings.evidence: Reproduced live: daemon logs 'refusing a connection from an unverified peer'; the client sees EOF.
findings.nextAction: A version/identity handshake so the daemon can say 'I am an older build, restart me' instead of hanging up.

findings.title: Windows has no peer verification and no real ACL
findings.problem: AF_UNIX on Windows exposes no peer-credential API, and os.Chmod only toggles the read-only attribute.
findings.impact: On Windows, nothing verifies that a caller is Nim, and socket confidentiality rests on default directory ACLs.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/peer/image_windows.go returns unsupported by design. Nothing in this project has ever been run on Windows.
findings.nextAction: A named-pipe transport with GetNamedPipeClientProcessId and an explicit DACL — a real architecture change.

findings.title: The journal chain is unkeyed
findings.problem: Nothing in the chain is secret, so anyone able to write nim.db can recompute every hash from the genesis.
findings.impact: A local attacker can rewrite history and the result verifies cleanly. This is integrity, not authenticity.
findings.evidence: docs/journal-format.md states it. --expect-head is the only cover, and only for what was committed before the head you recorded.
findings.nextAction: Decide before M8: a key the agent cannot reach, or a dashboard that presents the record as 'what this machine reported'.

findings.title: Policy lives in config.toml
findings.problem: The deny list is read from a file, breaking the standing decision that SQLite is the only thing an authorization decision reads.
findings.impact: Anything able to write that file can empty the policy, and the change leaves no journal entry.
findings.evidence: Fixed 2026-09-14: rules live in nim_rules, are changed with nim policy through the peer-verified socket, and every change is a rule.add or rule.remove entry in the chain. config.toml with a [policy] section is refused by every command, so the move cannot go unnoticed.
findings.nextAction: None. Kept because it is the record of what config.toml used to hold, and of why nothing an authorization decision reads may go back there.

findings.title: A credential is handed to the connector
findings.problem: The secret is injected into the downstream's environment, and the downstream inherits the relay's whole environment.
findings.impact: A compromised connector has its own credential and cannot be revoked. On Linux any same-user process can read it from /proc.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/shim/shim.go buildDownstreamCmd appends to os.Environ().
findings.nextAction: Process inversion: the daemon spawns the connector and holds the credential.

findings.title: Enrolment is as privileged as running Nim
findings.problem: Anything that can execute the binary as this user can enrol an agent or replace an existing enrolment.
findings.impact: Now that rules are scoped to enrolments and can grant, re-enrolling a name against another executable moves that name's rules, allow rules included, to the new program. Both the rule and the enrolment change are in the chain, so it is visible afterwards; it is not prevented.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/daemon/agent.go says so in its own comment; docs/decisions/0002 states what an enrolment is worth.
findings.nextAction: Needs a second OS principal to close: the daemon owning the enrolments as a user the agent is not. Not a journaling problem any more.

findings.title: The relay rig has not been re-run since M1.5
findings.problem: The end-to-end proof that a real client cannot tell it is going through Nim requires fastmcp, which is not installed here.
findings.impact: Byte-exactness currently rests on unit tests plus a run from before the merge.
findings.evidence: Re-run on 2026-09-15 against the current binary with fastmcp 4.0.3 in the rig's own venv: RESULT: IDENTICAL on every case that must not differ, and two cases that must differ through Nim asserted precisely -- a call a rule denies comes back as Nim's tool error, and a frame with a repeated method key is refused. A relay-rig CI job now runs it on every push; that job has not yet run on GitHub's runners, only locally.
findings.nextAction: Watch the first relay-rig job on GitHub go green. Until then the CI part of this is reasoned, not observed.

findings.title: Socket permissions have a window at creation
findings.problem: net.Listen creates the socket with the process umask; chmod 0600 follows immediately after.
findings.impact: A brief window where the socket is connectable by other local users. Peer verification still refuses them.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/daemon/daemon.go listen().
findings.nextAction: Set a restrictive umask around the Listen call.

findings.title: CI does not run go vet for Windows
findings.problem: Cross-compile jobs run go build only, so test files that break on Windows are not caught.
findings.impact: A portability break in test code reaches main. This happened once already.
findings.evidence: Found by running GOOS=windows go vet locally during M4 step 2. Fixed: every cross-compile job now runs go vet as well as go build. Confirmed in CI run 31576458402 — the windows/amd64 job shows a `Vet windows/amd64 :: success` step with GOOS=windows in its environment, and all three platforms are clean.
findings.nextAction: None. Kept on the page because a fixed finding is how the next person learns that go build alone never sees a _test.go file.

findings.title: A skipped adversarial test was indistinguishable from a passing one
findings.problem: CI did not pass -v, so a package whose adversarial tests all skipped printed the same 'ok' as one where they all passed. Looked at properly the exposure was wider than the path-swap test: there are fourteen t.Skip call sites and they guard the load-bearing ones — the impostor and non-Nim-process tests skip without python3, the agent derivation test skips if it cannot read its own parent.
findings.impact: The dashboard could go on calling a property verified while nothing had checked it for weeks.
findings.evidence: Fixed in two parts: CI now runs go test -race -v with pipefail, and assert-evidence-ran.sh fails the build if any test cited for a verified guarantee or a defended attack was skipped rather than run. Confirmed in CI run 31576458402 — ubuntu reports 57 cited tests ran with 1 build-tagged out and 0 skipped, macOS reports 58 ran and 0 skipped. The refusal itself was mutation-tested: rewriting one PASS line to SKIP in a real log makes the script exit 1 naming that test.
findings.nextAction: None. The check is the standing guard — absent is still allowed because a darwin-only test genuinely does not exist on linux, but skipped is not, because skipped is the state that looks like success.

decisions.title: What granularity is an 'agent'?
decisions.question: Client program (kernel-backed, coarse) or workspace/instance (finer, forgeable by the same user)?
decisions.resolution: Client program. Kernel-backed and honest; two windows of one program are the same agent.

decisions.title: What may an unknown agent do?
decisions.question: Once grants exist, is an unenrolled spawner denied, or does it fall back to the global policy?
decisions.resolution: A session no enrolment matched is bound by the rules that name no agent, and by nothing else. Rules only deny, so enrolment can only take capabilities away: an unenrolled program has exactly the ceiling every session had before agents existed, and nobody gains by avoiding enrolment. docs/decisions/0002 is the argument. It has to be answered again for allow rules, which are M4.5. Answered again for the allow model on 2026-09-15 in docs/decisions/0003: with nim policy default deny plus an agent-scoped allow, enrolment is what grants and an unenrolled program is denied by the default.

decisions.title: Should the hosted dashboard be publicly reachable?
decisions.question: It lists known weaknesses and attack paths for a private repository, so an unauthenticated URL publishes them.
decisions.resolution: Public, deliberately. Sergi turned deployment protection off so the page can be read by anyone. That is a decision about this page only -- it is written to be public, states its own limits, and carries no runtime data, no secrets and no local paths, all of which is enforced at build time rather than promised. It does not extend to anything else the project publishes. Audited end to end after deploying: see F-012 for the one way the deployment is broader than intended.

decisions.title: Does the journal get a key before M8?
decisions.question: Syncing an unkeyed record to a dashboard exports a liability rather than evidence.
decisions.resolution: Undecided. Either the journal gains a key the agent cannot reach, or M8 presents the record as 'what this machine reported'.

decisions.title: Should the public page be search-indexed?
decisions.question: Public and indexed are different things. The build still sends X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive, nosnippet, so the page is readable by anyone given the link but will not appear in search results.
decisions.resolution: Left as noindex, which is the reversible direction: a page can be indexed later, but it cannot be reliably un-indexed once crawled and archived. Worth a deliberate answer rather than a default, given the page is a list of this project's weaknesses.

milestones.name: Pass-through
milestones.objective: Relay stdio byte-for-byte and record every tools/call.
limitations: Nothing blocked, no credentials, no policy.

milestones.name: Trustworthy record
milestones.objective: Make the journal evidence rather than a log.
limitations: Integrity, not authenticity. The chain is unkeyed.

milestones.name: Minimal enforcement
milestones.objective: Refuse a tools/call before it reaches a connector.
limitations: Policy is a list of exact tool names in config.toml, which is F-004 and is M4's work rather than unfinished M2 work.

milestones.name: Daemon lifetime and socket identity
milestones.objective: A daemon that outlives a client session, and a socket where both ends know who the other is.
limitations: No peer verification on Windows.

milestones.name: Credentials
milestones.objective: Hold connector credentials outside the client's configuration.
limitations: PATH resolution on the registered command.
The credential is handed to the connector.

milestones.name: Agent identity + policy in SQLite
milestones.objective: Give a decision a subject, and move policy where an authorization input belongs.
deliverables: nim_rules + nim policy CLI, rules scoped per agent and connector
every rule change a chain entry
policy out of config.toml, and a stale section refused
two real agents against one connector receive different verdicts
limitations: Rules only denied until M4.5.
Two windows of one program are the same agent.
Enrolment changes were not journaled until 2026-09-15 (F-018, closed).

milestones.name: Allow rules and precedence
milestones.objective: Allow as well as deny, with a precedence stated in one function and shown by nim policy explain, without a policy language.
deliverables: defaults with nim policy default deny|allow, scoped like any rule
journal.Decide: most specific wins, deny beats allow, no rule means allow
nim policy allow / default / explain, and remove --default
policy.explain daemon request behind the CLI
nim_rules CHECK widened by a rebuild existing databases survive
D-002 answered again for the allow model (docs/decisions/0003)
limitations: No conditions on arguments, no time bounds, no budgets: those need a language or a counter, and are M5 and later.
Cedar was not needed for this; the spike stays deferred until something a precedence cannot express is wanted.

milestones.name: Budgets
milestones.objective: Per session, decremented at authorization time, not at execution time.
deliverables: a budget is a cap on ALLOWED calls per session, scoped like a rule: (agent, connector, tool or every tool)
checked in daemon.answer only once the rules have allowed the call: a budget narrows, never grants
the count is of allow/approved decisions, never outcomes, so a call the relay gave up on still spent its share and a refusal never does
nim_budgets outside the chain, every change one transaction with a budget.add / budget.remove entry
schema_version 4: canonical_encode_v4, field 20 budget_calls; existing databases rebuilt on open
nim policy budget <n> --tool <tool>|--all-tools [--agent] [--connector], nim policy budget remove, a BUDGETS table in nim policy list, matching budgets in nim policy explain
limitations: Per session means one relay run: a client that restarts its relay starts with a fresh count, on purpose; a cap meant to survive restarts needs a different subject than a session.
No time bounds and no conditions on arguments: every allowed call costs one unit.

What the client is told is the same policy refusal as for a rule, and the journal records the decision, not its reason: the sentence naming the budget exists only on the daemon's answer to the relay. A refusal by a budget and a refusal by a rule read alike in nim log.

milestones.name: Human approval
milestones.objective: Out-of-band prompt showing real parameters, never a model-generated summary.
deliverables: a third rule effect, ask: nim policy ask <tool> [--agent] [--connector] and nim policy default ask; precedence deny > ask > allow at equal specificity, in journal.Decide
the daemon answers a held call pending with a hold id and keeps it in memory only: tool, agent, connector, digest, the real arguments, the time
the relay sends the real params.arguments bytes once, in a call.arguments event, and waits on the same connection up to [daemon] approval_timeout (default 2m)
nim approve lists held calls with their real arguments, pretty-printed, every byte shown as itself; nim approve <id> and nim reject <id> [--reason] decide one
an approve is refused until the relay's report of the arguments has reached the daemon, and the first report is the one shown and approved; a reject goes through regardless
the decision is written to the journal as approved or rejected before the relay is told; on approval the relay forwards the exact original bytes
a session ending, its connection dropping, or the timer running out all reject and journal the call, so none is left neither approved nor rejected
the human's reason is returned to the CLI and logged by the daemon, never journaled; the arguments never reach the journal or a log line
limitations: Anyone who can run nim as this user can approve a call: the approval defends against the model driving the client, not against the operator, and a model that has been given a shell is indistinguishable from the operator on the socket.
Held calls live in the daemon's memory; a daemon killed outright loses them with no journal trace, and the relay then denies them locally.
No notification: an operator learns of a held call by running nim approve. No delegation, no queueing beyond the timeout, no conditions on arguments that would ask automatically.
A budget is not consulted for a call an ask rule holds: a human's approval is not subject to the cap, though the approved call counts toward it for the session's later allowed calls.
